newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD - SOUTH AFRICA OCT CPI SEEN NEAR NINE PCT.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD - SOUTH AFRICA OCT CPI SEEN NEAR NINE PCT.

text.p: The release of consumer inflation and trade data this week will provide shaky markets with a clearer picture of where inflation will peak this year and the state of the current account, economists said at the weekend.

A Reuters poll of eight economists forecast the October consumer price index would rise 8.8 percent year-on-year -- its highest level since July 1995 -- or 0.7 percent month-on-month, after a worse-than-expected 8.4 percent and 1.0 percent rise in September.
The consensus was drawn from a range of 8.6 to 9.0 percent.
The main culprit in the latest data was expected to be a continuing rise in food prices.
Food inflation rose 10.4 percent year-on-year in September after a 7.9 percent increase in August.
"Food prices will keep on increasing because of the Christmas season although the increase in meat prices is starting to slow down," said Sanlam economist Peter Calitz.
He added that it was likely there would be a slowdown in food prices and the overall inflation rate only from the second half of next year.
Technical factors would also play a part -- CPI rose 6.3 percent year-on-year and 0.3 percent month-on-month in October last year, economists said.
They said higher world oil prices and the lagged effects of the rand's depreciation against the dollar since February this year would weigh on the figure.
A number of periodic surveys -- such as reading matter and stationary, and hairdressing services and washing prices -- would bring further pressure to bear on the latest data.

Factors that were seen helping the figure were the 0.25 percentage point cut in the prime rate at the beginning of October although this was seen partly offset by additional value added tax on financial services.
Looking ahead, economists predicted a further rise in the inflation number in November.
"However, after November we're probably going to range-trade between 8.5 percent and 9.5 percent (year-on-year) for the next six months," said Herman van Papendorp of SMK Securities.
Most expected consumer inflation to peak at between 9.1 to 9.3 percent in November/December.
The latest data will be released at 0900 GMT on Wednesday.
October trade data, due for release from Tuesday onwards, drew a consensus forecast of a 900 million rand surplus compared with a 666.7 million rand surplus in September.
Economists were again wary to predict the figure which has been notoriously erratic in the past.
The few that could be drawn were more optimistic than in the past.

"All in all I'm looking at quite a bullish figure indicating that the (import) volume effect of the weaker exchange rate is starting to come through and that we are starting to see a more synchronised upswing with our major trading partners," said van Papendorp.
Sanlam's Calitz noted that the non-farming sector of the economy was slowing down, especially the manufacturing sector, which would also lead to lower import volumes.
"I'm more optimistic...the current account will still be in deficit but the trade account should show a much better surplus this time around," he said.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said this month the economic position in South Africa was stabilising and the current account deficit would have narrowed sharply in the third quarter.
However, he cautioned that last month's sharp fall in the rand had distorted the situation again.
The Reserve Bank is due to publish its next Quarterly Bulletin containing third quarter data on December 5.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
